newsitem.title: UK: Buba offical spells out Waigel gold discount plan.
newsitem.headline: Buba offical spells out Waigel gold discount plan.

text.p: Germany's gold reserves would be revalued at 60 percent of their market value under the proposal from Finance Miniter Theo Waigel, according to Bundesbank Council member Reimut Jochimsen.
The 40-percent discount to market gold value would match Germany's gold reserve calculation with those of Switzerland which announced a similar plan earlier this year.
"The lasting damage which the realisation of the gold plans would bring is far greater than the short-term financial benefit it is calculated to achieve," Jochimsen warned.
He said that the government's plans to revalue gold and currency reserves would actually end up causing overall interest rates to rise.
Germany's reserves of around 3,000 tonnes are valued at an acquisition cost of $93 per ounce. Gold was fixed on Friday afternoon at $345.60 per ounce.
The Waigel plan would increase their value to over $207 per ounce or over $19 billion from the current $8.8 billion.
"The (German) plan is very prudent and in line with the Swiss, perhaps that's not a coincidence," said Union Bank of Switzerland bullion makrket analyst Andy Smith.
All the other major European Union economies have their gold reserves valued in some relationship to the market and update the valuation figure regularly.
The Netherlands, for example, revalues every three years to an average of the last three years' London bullion market daily fixings minus 30 percent.
Italy revalues quarterly at the average of the last two or six months fixings which ever is the lower.
Only Luxembourg and Sweden have gold at a valuation unrelated to the market.

"A discount to the market price protects the downside," Smith said, explaining if the revaluation was used to add to asset liability and used to create money, then a price fall would have the opposite effect.

The fiercely conservative and independent Bundesbank on Wednesday rejected the plan to revalue the country's gold to help fill a budget deficit and bring Germany into contention for the start of European Monetary Union in 1999.

Since then officials of the government in Bonn and the bank in Frankfurt have exchanged views publicly and commentators have fulminated for and mainly against the plan in one of Germany's highest profile political pile ups in a generation.
Jochimsen said the German government's plans to revalue Bundesbank currency and gold reserves would constrain the central bank's activities in the run-up to EMU.
Along with Germany, Switzerland has been regarded as a pillar of economic orthodoxy and a supporter of gold rserves being kept as an anti-inflationary asset of last resort.
The Swiss even proposed selling part of the revalued reserves if a referendum passes a sceptical public and passes into law.
News that these countries would even discuss gold reserves let alone revalue or sell them has deeply shocked the bullion market.

"Anything linking central banks and gold reserves has a negative image (for the gold market)," said Robert Pringle, a consultant to the World Gold Council and editor of Central Banking, a quarterly journal.
--Brian Spoors London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
